summary: Reports which ARPANET sites Rand had contacted by July 15, 1971, and which network software elements had been verified at each. The matrix covers items such as the NCP, ICP, Telnet user and server programs and the log-on procedure.

plainLanguage.summary: This report shows which network software checks had been verified at each listed ARPANET site by July 15, 1971. Notes explain implementation differences and cases where a site had not been tested directly.

questions: which arpanet sites were checked in july 1971
what does the network checkout matrix show
subtitle: A matrix of ARPANET sites and the network software elements verified at each one.

tldr.problem: Network participants needed a record of which sites had verified host software and service functions.
tldr.mechanism: The authors list the sites contacted by July 15 and mark which NCP, ICP, Telnet, log-on and service checks were verified.
tldr.outcome: The report describes a dated status snapshot and notes several implementation differences. It was updated by RFC 198.

today: RFC 193 is listed as Unknown and was updated by RFC 198. It is a report on software verification at a particular time, not a protocol specification.

sections.title: The Network Checkout Matrix
sections.content:
As of July 15, the authors at Rand had contacted or been contacted by the sites in the report. A matrix records which elements of network software had been verified at each site.

The columns cover NCP, ICP, user and server Telnet, a Telnet-like protocol, log-on procedure and access to services. An x indicates that an element was verified; the MIT-645 entry is marked partial.
sections.plainLanguage: The report uses a table to show which software checks had been verified at each site. A mark means the authors confirmed that element.

sections.title: Results and Verification Limits
sections.content:
The matrix shows different levels of verification among the sites. The report notes that some software was reported to be working but had not been verified because of hardware difficulties or lack of testing.

For example, the authors had not verified the reported software at LL-67 and had not verified most software at MIT-645. The Utah tests took place before TENEX was being installed there.
sections.plainLanguage: A blank table entry does not always mean software failed. In some cases the authors had heard it worked but had not confirmed it themselves.

sections.title: Implementation Differences
sections.content:
The report describes a Telnet-like protocol at SRI-10 and BBN-10 that used a different line ending from Telnet. It says the sites planned to correct the difference. At BBN-10, the ICP could also produce a zero byte size under certain conditions.

Some sites reported that TENEX used the same local socket for multiple server connections. Ray Tomlinson said this was intentional. The report also states that BBN TENEX was being used over the network for some non-network work.
sections.plainLanguage: The notes identify differences in line endings and an ICP condition at two sites. They also explain that one behavior some users questioned was intentional.
